visitTitle: Annual check-up — post-sepsis recovery and prediabetes

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Good morning — Mr. Larson? Dick? Come on in, grab whichever chair looks least uncomfortable.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Morning, Doc. Dick's fine. Feels strange being in a clinic that isn't attached to an ICU, I'll say that.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I bet. I was reading through your chart before you came in. You had a rough stretch — the sepsis admission, septic shock, time on the ventilator with the ARDS. That's about as sick as a person gets. How have you been since discharge?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Honestly? Better than I was, worse than I'd like. Stairs still take something out of me. But I walk every day now. My daughter calls it my grandpa lap — once around the block, slow and dignified.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I will take a grandpa lap over a couch any day of the week. Any fevers since you got home? Chills, night sweats, anything that felt like an infection trying to come back?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, nothing like that. Knock on wood.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Chest pain? Trouble breathing when you're just sitting still?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No. I get winded on hills, and if I try to jog the dog gets embarrassed for me, but at rest I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Cough?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Not really. The lungs feel quieter than they used to, if that makes any sense.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: It does, and it fits — recovery from ARDS can take a full year, and you sound like you're tracking the right direction. They also found you anemic in the hospital. Any dizziness, racing heart, people telling you that you look pale?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The opposite, actually. My wife says I finally got my color back around March. No dizziness.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Good. So today is a check-up in the proper sense — we'll go over your medication list, look at the bloodwork from this morning, run a few screening questionnaires, and talk about the bigger picture. Sound all right?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Sure. I've got nowhere to be. Which is sort of the problem, actually.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Say more about that?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I got let go in February. Officially it was restructuring. Unofficially, I was out four months with the whole ICU adventure, and when I came back half my accounts had been handed off. Logistics doesn't wait around for you. So — unemployed. First time since I was sixteen years old.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I'm sorry. That's a real loss, on top of everything your body already went through. How are you filling the days?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Job applications, mostly. Some daytime television I'm not proud of. Money-wise we're okay — my wife's job carries the household fine, so it's not about the paycheck. It's that I used to talk to thirty people a day, and now I mostly talk to the dog. He's a poor conversationalist.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That kind of isolation matters to your health as much as most things I can measure. Do you see friends? Family outside the house?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Not much anymore. The guys from work stopped calling around the time I stopped being useful to them. And the house is full — six of us, with the kids and my mother-in-law — but full and connected aren't the same thing, you know?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I do know. And how's the house itself treating you? Last visit there was a note that the housing situation was a strain.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: It's too small, plain and simple. Three bedrooms, six people. The landlord takes his sweet time with repairs — the bathroom fan has been dead since winter, there's a window that won't close right. We keep looking, but there's nothing decent in our range near the kids' school.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Okay. Part of today's visit is a formal assessment of health and social care needs, so I'm going to document the housing situation and the job loss, and I'll have the front desk print our community resource sheet — there's an employment center and a tenant advocacy line on it. Not magic, but people do actually use them.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Can't hurt. Beats talking to the dog.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Let me run the screening questions. Over the past two weeks, how often have you been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A few days, I'd say. Not most days. Job hunting is a grind, but I still enjoy my kids, cooking, the ballgame.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: And feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Not hopeless, no. Frustrated, absolutely. But not that.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That puts you at one point out of six on the short mood screen, which is low — reassuring. But given the year you've had, I want a deal: if that changes, you tell me. Not the dog, me.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Deal.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Substance questions — I ask everyone, every time. Any drug use in the past twelve months? Marijuana, pills that weren't prescribed to you, anything else?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No. A beer at a barbecue is about as wild as I get these days.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Tobacco, ever?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Never. My dad smoked enough for the entire family tree. Cured me before I started.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Your drug screening questionnaire comes out to a zero, so nothing to chase there. Now, medications — the chart flagged you as due for a medication review. What are you actually taking, day to day?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Day to day? Nothing regular. When I left the hospital they whittled the list down and then off entirely at the follow-ups. That's it.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: So no daily prescription medications at all right now.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Correct. It's the emptiest my bathroom shelf has looked in a year.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then I'll reconcile the list — it was still showing some hospital leftovers, and cleaning that up genuinely matters. Any medication allergies?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: None that anyone's ever found.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: All right, exam time. Deep breath for me... again... good. Heart sounds regular. Let me see the ankles... no swelling. Your blood pressure today is 107 over 69, which is excellent. Heart rate 63, breathing 15 times a minute, nice and easy. Any pain right now, zero to ten?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A one, maybe. The low back mutters when I sit too long. It's background noise.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Noted. Weight came in at 84.4 kilos, height 166.8, so the BMI works out to 30.34 — just over the obesity line. I mention it not to nag, but because it connects directly to the next thing. Your labs from this morning are back. The hemoglobin A1c — the three-month average of your blood sugar — is 5.99 percent. That keeps you in prediabetes territory.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Still? I half figured almost dying would have burned some sugar off.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Ha — it stubbornly doesn't work that way. Here's the good news: your glucose today was 86.7, completely normal, and the rest of the metabolic panel looks solid. Sodium 139, potassium 4.89, chloride and bicarbonate fine. Kidneys came through at a creatinine of 1.22 with a BUN of 13.78 — I always double-check kidneys after a septic shock episode, and yours held up.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: That is genuinely good to hear. Kidneys were the daily topic in the ICU. That and my lungs.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: They took the hit and recovered. So prediabetes is the one thing on this panel we can still steer. Normal A1c is under 5.7; you're at 5.99. Five to seven percent weight loss — for you that's roughly four to six kilos — plus stretching that daily walk out, and this number very often drifts back to normal.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: So the grandpa laps get longer.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Longer and more frequent. I'd rather see thirty minutes most days than one heroic hour on Saturday. And frankly, a daily walking routine will help the job-hunt brain too. Structure is going to be your friend this year — for the sugar, the weight, and the mood.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Structure. I used to schedule forty truck routes a day. I suppose I can schedule myself.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That's the spirit — you're the last remaining account, manage yourself well. One more housekeeping item: you missed your flu shot in the fall, and I'd like to get you covered while you're here. Any bad reaction to flu vaccines before?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, I just forget them. Fine. Which arm do they want?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: The nurse will sort that out — it's the standard trivalent one, sore arm for a day at most. So, the summary: prediabetes — lifestyle push, recheck the A1c in about six months. Weight — aiming for that five percent. The anemia from the hospitalization — you look well and have no symptoms, we'll keep following it. Job, housing, isolation — resource sheet today, and you keep me honest about your mood. Flu shot before you leave. Questions for me?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Just one. The tiredness — is that the anemia, the lungs, or the unemployment?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Truthfully? Probably a share of each, and all three should keep improving. If the fatigue plateaus or gets worse instead, we look harder at it. Fair?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Fair. Thanks, Doc. This was less depressing than I budgeted for.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That's the review headline I want. Sit tight, the nurse is coming with your vaccine, and the front desk will book your follow-up.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Left. The right one is my resume-clicking arm.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: After a ventilator, I think I can survive a sore shoulder.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Thank you both. Time for grandpa lap number two — the parking lot.

soap.subjective: Dick Larson is a 37-year-old man presenting for a routine check-up, his first comprehensive outpatient visit since recovering from a hospitalization for sepsis complicated by septic shock and acute respiratory distress syndrome. He reports steadily improving stamina since discharge: he walks daily and tolerates level ground well but remains exertionally limited on hills and stairs. He denies fever, chills, night sweats, cough, chest pain, dyspnea at rest, palpitations, orthopnea, and leg swelling. Regarding his known anemia, he denies dizziness or pallor and notes his family feels his color has returned. He rates pain 1/10, attributed to intermittent low back ache with prolonged sitting. Interval social history is significant: he lost his logistics job in February after his prolonged medical leave and is unemployed for the first time in his adult life. He describes markedly reduced social contact since the illness, though household finances remain stable on his wife's income. He lives with five family members in a three-bedroom rental with delayed landlord maintenance and describes the housing situation as unsatisfactory and crowded. He denies persistent low mood or anhedonia. He has never smoked, drinks alcohol rarely, and denies any drug use. He takes no daily prescription medications; a medication review was due and completed today. No known allergies.
soap.objective:
Vitals: BP 107/69 mmHg, HR 63/min, RR 15/min, weight 84.4 kg, height 166.8 cm, BMI 30.34 kg/m2, pain score 1/10.
Exam: Well-appearing, comfortable, conversant. Lungs clear bilaterally without increased work of breathing. Heart regular rate and rhythm. No conjunctival pallor. No lower extremity edema.
Labs: Hemoglobin A1c 5.99%. Basic metabolic panel: glucose 86.7 mg/dL, BUN 13.78 mg/dL, creatinine 1.22 mg/dL, calcium 9.98 mg/dL, sodium 139.13 mmol/L, potassium 4.89 mmol/L, chloride 104.04 mmol/L, total CO2 28.05 mmol/L.
Screenings: PHQ-2 total score 1. DAST-10 total score 0. PRAPARE completed: household of 6; reported annual family income $198,810.
soap.plan:
### Prediabetes
A1c 5.99% remains in the prediabetic range with a normal fasting glucose of 86.7 mg/dL.
- Lifestyle counseling provided: goal of 5–7% weight loss and progressive daily walking.
- Repeat A1c at follow-up in approximately 6 months.

### Body mass index 30+ — obesity
BMI 30.34 kg/m2 today.
- Dietary moderation and graded aerobic activity as tolerated post-ARDS.
- Weight recheck at follow-up.

### Post-sepsis recovery (sepsis, septic shock, ARDS) and anemia
Functional recovery is progressing; no red-flag symptoms of recurrent infection. Renal indices reassuring after septic shock (creatinine 1.22 mg/dL). Known anemia is clinically asymptomatic today.
- Continue graduated activity; return precautions reviewed for fever, dyspnea, or declining stamina.
- Continue longitudinal monitoring of anemia and fatigue trajectory.

### Unemployment, social isolation, and unsatisfactory housing
Newly documented unemployment and social isolation; ongoing unsatisfactory housing. Assessment of health and social care needs completed today.
- Community resource sheet provided (employment center, tenant advocacy line).
- Encouraged structured daily routine and social re-engagement; patient agreed to report mood changes.

### Medication review due
Medication reconciliation completed; residual hospital entries removed. No active daily prescriptions.
- Continue as-needed self-care only; revisit list at next visit.

### Preventive care and screening
Depression screening negative (PHQ-2 score 1); drug abuse screening negative (DAST-10 score 0); never-smoker. Substance use assessment unremarkable.
- Influenza vaccine (split virus, trivalent, preservative-free) administered today.
- Follow-up visit in approximately 6 months, sooner for any concerns.

• Encouraged structured daily routine and social re-engagement; patient agreed to report mood changes.

visitTitle: General adult exam — new hypertension and metabolic syndrome
clinician: GREATER LAWRENCE FAMILY HEALTH CENTER INC

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Mr. Wisozk? I'm Dr. Okafor. Good to finally put a face to the chart — I believe my colleague has mostly seen you for the B12 injections.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: That's me. Elias. The human pincushion. And you can thank my brother for this appointment — he said, Eli, you're fifty-four, you haven't had a proper physical in years, go before something finds you first. He nags, I comply. It's our system.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Your brother and I are going to get along. Is anything actually bothering you today, or is this purely the brother-mandated tune-up?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Mostly the tune-up. Although — two things, since you're asking. I get these dull headaches at the back of my head some mornings. And my gums bleed when I brush. Nothing dramatic. Just a pink sink, most days.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Both worth looking at, I'm glad you mentioned them. The headaches first — how long has that been going on?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A few months? They fade by lunchtime. I blamed the sofa bed, honestly. I sleep on my sister's sofa bed these days, so it's suspect number one for everything.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: You're staying with your sister — tell me about the setup.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Her house, her husband, their two kids, and me. Five of us. I stopped working last year and I'm not looking, to be straight with you. My mother was sick for a long time — I was her person, day and night, until she passed last fall. After that I just... didn't go back. The warehouse says the door's open. I'm not ready to walk through it yet. So my own income this year is next to nothing — a few thousand dollars, odd jobs. My sister feeds me, I fix everything in her house that breaks. It's a fair trade, mostly.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That's an enormous year — the caregiving, losing your mother, leaving work, moving households. How are you carrying all that?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Some days heavy, some days fine. I sleep okay-ish on the famous sofa. I wouldn't call myself depressed. Tired of my own company, sometimes.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Let me ask the standard screening questions, everyone gets them. Past two weeks — little interest or pleasure in doing things?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Several days, I'd say. Not most.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Several days. It comes with the grief, I think. It visits, it leaves.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: And the worry side — feeling nervous, anxious, on edge?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Here and there. When I think about money, or what I'm doing with myself. A few days a week, maybe a low hum.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Trouble stopping the worry once it starts?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Not really. I put on a game or fix a cabinet and it lets go.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Those answers put you at a two on the depression screen and a three on the anxiety scale — both low, not in a range where I'd push treatment. Grief keeps its own schedule. If it gets heavier, that's a conversation, not a confession. All right?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A conversation, not a confession. I like that. Deal.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Alcohol — how often, how much?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Two or three evenings a week I'll have a beer or two with my brother-in-law, watching the game. Rarely more than that. I'm asleep by ten, I'm a cheap date.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That scores a three on the alcohol screen — below the level we worry about for men, so just keep it where it is. Tobacco, ever?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Never. I watched my uncle go from cigarettes. That vaccinated the whole family.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Any drug use? Marijuana, pills not prescribed to you?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, nothing.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Good. Now the numbers, because a couple of them matter today. Your blood pressure is 141 over 100 — and I rechecked it myself after you'd been sitting a while, same story. The bottom number especially is high. Heart rate's 100 today too.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The sofa bed strikes again?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I wish I could blame the sofa. Between today's readings and how consistent they are, this is real — essential hypertension, high blood pressure as its own condition. And it doesn't travel alone. Your weight is 93.9 kilos, BMI 30.21, so over the obesity line. Your A1c came back at 6.28 percent — that's prediabetes, drifting the wrong direction. Glucose today was 91, which is fine day-to-day. Kidneys look good — creatinine 1.12, BUN 17.36. Sodium 139, potassium 3.97.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A lot of numbers. Give me the plain version.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Plain version: high blood pressure, blood sugar creeping, weight over the line. That cluster has a name — metabolic syndrome. Each piece nudges the others, and together they raise the risk for heart disease, stroke, and diabetes down the road. The flip side: they also improve together.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A syndrome. Wonderful. My brother is going to be insufferable.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: He's entitled to exactly one told-you-so. Here's my plan, two moves at once. First, a medication: hydrochlorothiazide, 25 milligrams, one tablet every morning. It's a water pill — it lowers pressure by helping you offload salt and fluid.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Water pill meaning I'll be visiting the bathroom?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: More at first, which is why it's a morning pill, not a bedtime pill. Take it with breakfast. If you feel lightheaded when you stand, or you get muscle cramps, call us — it can nudge your potassium and sodium, so we'll recheck bloodwork after you've been on it a while.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Fine. One pill, mornings. I can manage that even on a sofa bed.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Second move — lifestyle, and I'll enroll you in our hypertension education program so it's not just me talking at you once a year. The short version: salt is the big lever. Deli meat, sausage, canned soups, chips —

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: You've just read out my grocery list.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then we've found our lever. Aim for cooking more of what you eat — you live with a family, cook for them, make it your job since you're the house fixer anyway. And walking: thirty minutes, most days. Take the kids' dog.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The dog is lazier than I am, but fine. What about the B12? Do I keep that going?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Yes — the B12 injections continue unchanged, that's for your anemia and it's doing its job. When was the last one?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Couple of weeks ago. I do notice when I skip — I get foggy and my legs feel like sandbags.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then stay on schedule. So let's make it official for the medication review: your list is the vitamin B12 injectable, and now hydrochlorothiazide 25 milligrams each morning. Anything else — vitamins, supplements, herbal anything?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Nothing else. Simplest list in the family.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Reconciled. Now open up for me — I want to look at those gums. Mm-hm. Yes — the gum line is puffy and bleeds with light contact. That's gingivitis. The good news is it's the reversible stage of gum disease, but it needs a proper dental cleaning, not just my opinion.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I haven't sat in a dentist's chair since before my mother got sick. Four years, maybe five.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then it's time. I'm sending a dental referral today — cleaning and an exam. Brush twice daily, soft brush, and floss even when it bleeds; the bleeding fades as the gums get healthier, usually within a couple of weeks.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Fine, fine. The dentist. My brother wins again.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: While you're here, you're also due for a flu shot. Any problems with those in the past?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No. Left arm, please — I already know the drill.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Perfect. And I want to see you back in about a month for a blood pressure recheck. If you can get hold of a home cuff, even better — measure in the morning, sitting, feet on the floor, and write the numbers down.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: My nephew has one of those gadget cuffs. He measures everything, that boy — steps, sleep, the dog's naps.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Borrow it. Bring me the log. Any other questions before the nurse comes in?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Just one. The morning headaches — is that the blood pressure?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Quite possibly — morning headaches and high pressure often travel together. My honest expectation is they fade as the numbers come down. If they don't, we take a harder look. Deal?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Deal. Thank you, Doctor. My brother will demand a full report at dinner.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Tell him the door prizes were a water pill and a dentist appointment, and that he gets exactly one told-you-so.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Painless. If only the dentist could promise the same.

soap.subjective: Elias Wisozk is a 54-year-old man presenting for a general examination, his first comprehensive visit in several years. He reports intermittent dull occipital headaches on waking over the past few months, resolving by midday, and daily gum bleeding with brushing. He denies chest pain, palpitations at rest, dyspnea, visual changes, focal weakness, dizziness, and syncope. No fevers, weight loss, polyuria, or polydipsia. Psychosocially, he left full-time work last year after a prolonged period caring for his mother, who died last fall; he is not currently seeking work and has minimal personal income, living in a five-person household with his sister's family. He endorses intermittent low mood and worry consistent with grief but denies persistent depression, anhedonia, or panic. He drinks 1–2 beers two to three evenings weekly, has never smoked, and denies drug use. Known anemia is managed with vitamin B12 injections, which he continues on schedule; he reports fatigue and leg heaviness when injections are missed. Medication review was due and completed today. No known allergies.

visitTitle: General exam — chronic low back pain and positive depression screen

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Emory? Come on back. I'm Dr. Reyes. Have a seat wherever. How's it going?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Fine. Good, I mean. Fine.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Two fines and a good — solid opening. It says you booked a general exam. Anything specific on your mind, or just due for a once-over?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Mostly due. I haven't really been to a doctor since college. And my back's been acting up again, so I figured I'd bundle it.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Efficient. Tell me about the back.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: It's the same low back thing I've had for a few years. Junior year I helped basically my roommate's entire floor move out in one day — couches, a mini fridge, somebody's weight set. Felt something pull. It never totally un-pulled, if that's a word.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: How would you describe it now — where, what kind of pain?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A dull band across the very bottom of my back. Right now it's like a four out of ten. Desk days make it worse. I do QA testing for a software company, so when a release is close it's ten hours in a chair, and by Friday I'm walking like a question mark.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Does it ever shoot down a leg? Numbness, tingling, weakness in the feet?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, nothing like that. It stays in the back.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Any trouble with bladder or bowels, fevers, night pain that wakes you, weight loss?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No. It's boring pain. Reliable, boring pain.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Boring is actually good news with backs. What helps?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Walking. Hot showers. I had ibuprofen for a while, which worked, but the bottle ran out months ago and I never dealt with it.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Okay, we'll deal with it today. Let's do the general once-over questions. You had your appendix out as a teenager, right?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Yeah, when I was fifteen. That's my only surgery. I've still got the scar and a mild distrust of gas station food.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Reasonable takeaways. Any medications at all right now?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Nothing. The empty ibuprofen bottle doesn't count, I assume.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: It counts as a plot point. Allergies?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: None.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Smoking, vaping?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Never. Neither.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Alcohol?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Occasionally. A beer with the roommates on weekends, if that.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Got it. This is also a screening visit, so everybody gets the questionnaires — mood, safety, substances. Some are personal; answer as honestly as you're comfortable. First one: over the last two weeks, how often have you had little interest or pleasure in doing things?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: ...Honestly? More than half the days. Probably most days.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Yeah. Most days, kind of a gray filter over everything. I figured it was just winter that never gave the keys back.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I appreciate you being straight with me — that answer flags the longer version, nine questions, same idea. Trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or sleeping too much?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Falling asleep, nearly every night. My brain does release retrospectives at 1 a.m.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Feeling tired or having little energy?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Nearly every day. Which I always blamed on the sleep thing.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Poor appetite or overeating?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I forget lunch more than half the time. Not on purpose.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Feeling bad about yourself — that you're a failure or have let people down?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Some days. Several, I guess.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Trouble concentrating on things like reading or screens?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: More than half the days, which is awkward, because concentrating on screens is the whole job.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Moving or speaking slowly, or the opposite — fidgety, restless?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Restless, several days. I bounce my knee enough that my deskmate filed a complaint. A friendly one.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Last one, and I ask everyone directly: thoughts that you'd be better off dead, or of hurting yourself in any way?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No. Never that. I want to be really clear on that one — no.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I'm glad, and I believe you. Adding it up, you score a 17, which lands in the moderately severe range for depressive symptoms.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Seventeen sounds like a lot when you say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: It's a number that says this deserves real attention — not a verdict, not a personality. How long has the gray filter been running?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Since winter, maybe? Work went into crunch — we shipped two releases back to back — and my girlfriend moved across the country for grad school in January, so evenings got really quiet. I figured it was stress. It is stress, mostly. I still function. I hit my deadlines.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Functioning and struggling aren't opposites — plenty of people do both at once, and you're describing textbook load: crunch, long-distance, isolation, bad sleep, back pain. Here's what I'd like to offer. One: counseling — a therapist is the best-studied tool for exactly this picture. I can give you a list that works with your insurance, including a couple that do evening telehealth.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I'm not really a talk-about-it guy. Clearly.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: And yet you just did it pretty well for ten minutes. I'm not going to force anything — you're safe, you're functioning, and this is your call. My ask is smaller: take the list, actually look at it, and come back in four weeks so we can re-score this and see the trend. If it's not budging, we talk options again — therapy, and there are medication options too if it ever comes to that. Nothing today unless you want it.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Four weeks and a list. That I can do.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Meanwhile, the boring powerful stuff: a fixed wake time even after bad nights, daylight in the morning, movement every day — your back will thank you too — and schedule the girlfriend calls like meetings so the quiet evenings have an anchor.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: She'd actually love that. She lives by her calendar.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Two more screens and we're done with questions. These I ask everyone: at home or in any relationship, is anyone humiliating you, making you afraid, hurting you physically, or forcing anything?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No. Nothing like that. We're long-distance but we're good, and the roommates are fine.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Good — that screen is a zero. Substances: any drug use in the past year? Cannabis, pills not prescribed to you, anything else?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A friend gave me a gummy once this winter when my back was bad and I couldn't sleep. Twice, total, honestly. Didn't love it, didn't repeat it.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Thanks for the honesty — that puts you at a one out of ten on the drug screen, which is low, and nothing there worries me. I'd rather give your back better tools anyway. Hop up on the table, let me examine you. Bend forward as far as comfortable... side to side... okay. Your low back muscles are tight on both sides, but the spine itself isn't tender, leg raises don't reproduce anything, strength and reflexes are all normal. That's a muscular, mechanical picture — consistent with the desk marathons.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Boring, reliable pain, like I said.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: One number I want you to know about: your blood pressure today is 136 over 94, which is higher than I want to see at twenty-two. One reading doesn't mean much — pain, coffee, and clinics all push it up — so we'll recheck at the four-week visit rather than react today. Heart rate's 89, everything else looks great, and at 77 kilos your BMI is 22.5, dead normal.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Huh. Okay. My dad has blood pressure stuff, so... noted.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Good to know, and all the more reason to just track it. Now, back plan: I'm prescribing ibuprofen 400 milligrams — take one with food when it flares, not on an empty stomach. It's the refill of your expired strategy, but legitimate this time. Plus the unglamorous part: out of the chair every hour, even five minutes. Walk at lunch. When you lift — hinge at the hips, keep the load close.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: My watch already yells at me to stand. I ignore it professionally.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: New policy: the watch outranks you. Last thing — open your mouth for me? Your gums are red and puffy along the edges, and I'd bet they bleed when you floss.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: When I remember to floss. Which is when it bleeds. Which is why I don't. It's a vicious cycle.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Classic gingivitis loop. It reverses with a real cleaning and daily flossing — the bleeding stops once the gums calm down, usually a couple of weeks. I'm sending a dental referral today.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: My hygienist ghost-writes my guilt already. Fine. Dentist, list, four weeks.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Perfect summary. And Emory — if the gray filter ever gets darker than what you told me today, especially anywhere near that last question I asked, you call us same-day or use the crisis line on the sheet. That's not a formality.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Understood. For real. Thanks for not making this weird.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Making it not-weird is most of the job. Front desk will book the four-week recheck — back, blood pressure, and mood score, all three.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The trilogy. See you in four weeks.

soap.subjective: Emory Kovacek is a 22-year-old man presenting for a general examination, his first in several years, with a concurrent flare of chronic low back pain. The pain is a dull band across the lower lumbar region, currently 4/10, dating to a lifting episode in college and clearly aggravated by prolonged sitting during work crunches as a software QA tester. It improves with walking and heat. He denies radicular symptoms, numbness, weakness, bowel or bladder dysfunction, night pain, fevers, and weight loss. He previously used ibuprofen with good effect but has none at home. Depression screening was notably positive: he endorses anhedonia and low mood most days since winter, initial insomnia, low energy, reduced appetite, intermittent guilt, poor concentration, and restlessness, in the context of work crunch and his girlfriend's cross-country move. He explicitly and credibly denies thoughts of death or self-harm. He remains functional at work. Domestic safety screen negative. Substance history: cannabis edible twice this past winter for pain/sleep, otherwise none; never smoked; occasional alcohol. Surgical history: appendectomy in adolescence. No medications; no known allergies.
soap.objective:
Vitals: BP 136/94 mmHg, HR 89/min, RR 15/min, weight 77 kg, height 185.2 cm, BMI 22.46 kg/m2, pain score 4/10.
Exam: Well-appearing, calm, appropriate affect; engages readily. Lumbar exam: bilateral paraspinal tightness without midline tenderness; flexion mildly limited by stiffness; straight-leg raise negative bilaterally; lower-extremity strength, sensation, and reflexes intact. Gait normal. Oral exam: erythematous, edematous gingival margins consistent with gingivitis. Well-healed right lower quadrant surgical scar.
Screenings: PHQ-2 total 5; PHQ-9 total 17 (moderately severe range; item 9 negative). HARK total 0. DAST-10 total 1. PRAPARE: 3-person household; reported annual family income $91,796.
soap.plan:
### Chronic low back pain
Mechanical, muscular pattern without red flags, aggravated by prolonged sitting; exam without neurologic deficit.
- Ibuprofen 400 mg oral tablet prescribed; take with food as needed for flares.
- Activity counseling: hourly breaks from sitting, daily walking, hip-hinge lifting mechanics.
- Reassess at 4-week follow-up.

### Stress with depressive symptoms
PHQ-2 of 5 reflexed to PHQ-9 of 17, moderately severe symptom burden in the setting of occupational crunch and social isolation; no suicidal ideation; functioning preserved. Documented as stress; will track closely.
- Counseling resource list provided (including telehealth options); patient agreed to review.
- Behavioral activation counseling: fixed wake time, morning light, daily movement, scheduled social contact.
- Repeat PHQ-9 at 4-week follow-up; discuss therapy and further options if not improving. Crisis-line information provided with explicit same-day return precautions.

### Gingivitis
Gingival erythema and edema with bleeding on flossing.
- Patient referral for dental care placed for cleaning and examination.
- Daily flossing and twice-daily brushing counseled.

### Elevated blood pressure reading

visitTitle: Annual general exam — prediabetes, hyperlipidemia, and knee osteoarthritis
clinician: PRIMARY CARE MEDICINE AND PEDIATRICS, LLC

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Mrs. Casas! Come in, come in. How is the garden doing this summer?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Doctor, the tomatoes are showing off. I brought a little bag for the front desk girls — don't worry, I washed them. The zucchini, on the other hand, I am at war with. You turn your back one day and it's the size of a baseball bat.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: You're single-handedly feeding this clinic. It's wonderful to see you. So today is your yearly check — the full once-over. How have you been feeling since last summer?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Thanks be to God, mostly good. I keep busy. Five of us in the house now — my daughter and the grandchildren moved in with me last year, you remember. She works nights at the hospital laundry, so I run the mornings. Lunches, school drop-off, the whole circus.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That's a full-time job in itself. Are you getting any time for yourself? Friends, church, neighbors?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Ah. Less than I should. By the time the little ones are asleep, I am also asleep. My friend Rosa calls, but visiting — no, not so much anymore. My world got small, Doctor. Busy, but small.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I hear you, and I want to keep an eye on that — a busy house and a small world can still be a lonely combination. How is the knee treating you? The arthritis.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Today, quiet. Zero complaints, if you can believe it. Summer is my friend — it's the winter when it creaks like my kitchen door. When it acts up I take the naproxen, the little blue ones from the pharmacy, 220, one with breakfast, and that settles it. Some weeks I take none at all.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That's exactly how I like to hear it used — as needed, with food. No stomach burning, no black stools, no swelling in the knee?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, no, and no. My stomach is made of old country material. Very durable.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Any chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No. I walk to the market and back, fifteen minutes each way, no problem. Uphill on the way home, I will add, for the record.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Noted for the record. Any dizziness, headaches, changes in your vision, numbness?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: How's your sleep? And your appetite?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I sleep like a stone until five, then the worrying shift begins. Lying there doing arithmetic — the bills, my daughter, my sister back home. Twenty minutes of nonsense, then I get up and make coffee and it goes away.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Let me ask the mood questions properly, I ask everyone. In the past two weeks, little interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, not at all. The garden alone keeps me in business.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No. Tired sometimes, but not sad-tired. Just tired-tired.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: And the worry — nervous, anxious, on edge?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A few days, yes. The five a.m. arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Trouble relaxing, or feeling something awful might happen?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Once in a while. When my sister doesn't answer the phone for two days, my head writes a whole telenovela. Then she calls and it's cancelled.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That puts your anxiety score at a five — mild territory. Worry that visits and leaves, like you say. If it ever starts staying — keeping you from sleep past those twenty minutes, or following you through the day — you tell me, yes?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Yes, yes. I promise.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Now, a few questions I ask every patient every year, and I ask them privately because they matter. Is anyone in your life humiliating you, frightening you, hurting you, or forcing you in any way?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, Doctor. And I know why you ask me especially. That was my first husband, many years ago, another lifetime. He is long gone from my life. In my house now it is me, my daughter, and three noisy angels. I am safe. I promise you that.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Thank you for answering it straight — I'll keep asking every year all the same, because that's the job.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Ask away. The answer will stay boring, God willing.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Any cigarettes? I know the answer, but for the record.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Ha! Two years of smoking when I was a teenager, to look interesting. It didn't work, so I quit. That was almost fifty years ago.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Longest-standing quit in my whole panel. Alcohol? Any drugs, marijuana, pills beyond what we know about?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A little cup of wine at Christmas. Otherwise no, nothing, never.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That drug screen is a zero, as always. Now — medications. The list says only the naproxen, the 220 milligram tablets, as needed for the knee. Anything else at home? Vitamins, teas, anything from the botánica?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Manzanilla tea, but that's for the soul, not the body. Otherwise just the naproxen. That's all.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Reconciled and official. Let's look at your numbers, because you earned some good ones. Blood pressure today: 135 over 82. The top number is a touch above perfect — not medicine territory, but we watch it. Heart rate 60 and steady, breathing 12, and your weight is 73.8 kilos.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Down! I was 78 once upon a time in that chart, I remember it.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Down indeed — your BMI is 27.7 now. The market walks and the war with the zucchini are working. Now the blood tests from this morning. Your sugar average — the A1c — is 6.11 percent. Still prediabetes, same neighborhood as last year, holding steady. Today's sugar was 79, which is lovely. Kidneys perfect — creatinine 0.68. Sodium 138, potassium 3.9.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: And the cholesterol? That's my inheritance, my mother had it too.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Your inheritance is behaving. Total cholesterol 168, the bad LDL is 87, the good HDL is 59, triglycerides 110. For someone with hyperlipidemia on the books, these are genuinely good numbers.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The oatmeal gets the credit. And less rice than before — my daughter measures it now like a pharmacist.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Keep the pharmacist on staff. Blood count: hemoglobin 16.9, hematocrit 47.6 — no sign of the old anemia today, your iron story looks closed. Platelets 351, white count 7.4, all in order.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: So the blood is rich again. Good. I told you the lentils would do it.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: You did tell me. Now open wide for me — I want to check your mouth. Mm. Your gums are puffy along the bottom, and they bleed a little when I touch them. Do they bleed when you brush?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A little pink when I spit, yes. I thought that was normal at my age.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: It's common, not normal — it's gingivitis, the early, fixable kind of gum disease. I'm sending you to the dentist for a proper cleaning.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Ay, the dentist. Fine. But I want it known I go under protest.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Duly recorded. Brush twice a day, soft brush, and don't stop when it bleeds — that part gets better in a couple of weeks. Now, one more thing: your flu shot. I know it's only August —

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Already? The children aren't even back in school!

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: You're here, the vaccine is here, and the calendar has a way of eating good intentions. Same one as every year, the trivalent.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Fine, fine. Left arm. The right one stirs the pots.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Perfect. So, the summary, Mrs. Casas: sugar — steady, keep the walks and the measured rice, we recheck next year. Cholesterol — excellent, keep the oatmeal. Knee — naproxen as needed with food is exactly right. Weight — moving the right way, well done. Mood — mild five a.m. worries, we keep an ear on it. Gums — dentist, under protest. Flu shot today. Questions for me?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Only one. The grandchildren bring home every germ ever invented. The flu shot covers me for their whole plague season?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That's exactly why we're doing it today — grandmother of three is a frontline occupation. Wash the hands, get the sleep, and you're as covered as I can make you.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Then jab me and I'll go liberate my tomatoes from the waiting room.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Flattery accepted. Same time next year, Doctor — God willing and the zucchini permitting.

soap.subjective: Eva Casas is a 62-year-old woman presenting for her annual general examination. She feels well overall. Her known osteoarthritis of the knee is currently asymptomatic (pain 0/10 today); she reports a winter-predominant pattern managed with over-the-counter naproxen as needed with food, without dyspepsia, melena, or knee swelling. She walks to the market daily (~30 minutes round trip). She denies chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, dizziness, headaches, visual changes, and focal numbness or weakness. Sleep is preserved except for brief early-morning rumination about finances and family; she endorses intermittent mild worry but no low mood, anhedonia, or hopelessness. She lives with her daughter and three grandchildren and provides substantial childcare; she acknowledges reduced peer contact, consistent with her documented limited social contact and social isolation. Given her remote history as a victim of intimate partner abuse, a private safety screen was conducted: she reports the relationship ended many years ago and states she feels safe at home. She is a refugee who resettled decades ago. Ex-smoker (brief use in adolescence, quit ~age 16); rare alcohol; denies drug use. Medications: naproxen sodium 220 mg oral tablet as needed. No known allergies.

Labs: A1c 6.11%; glucose 79.11 mg/dL; BUN 7.7 mg/dL; creatinine 0.68 mg/dL; calcium 9.23 mg/dL; sodium 138.23 mmol/L; potassium 3.94 mmol/L; chloride 107.69 mmol/L; CO2 23.26 mmol/L. Lipids: total cholesterol 168.51 mg/dL, LDL (direct) 87.17 mg/dL, HDL 59.18 mg/dL, triglycerides 110.82 mg/dL. CBC: WBC 7.42, hemoglobin 16.89 g/dL, hematocrit 47.59%, MCV 82.03 fL, platelets 351.89.

visitTitle: Prenatal intake visit — first trimester, newly identified anemia

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Knock knock — Hiedi? Hi, I'm Dr. Amari, one of the obstetricians here. Welcome. And you brought reinforcements?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Hi — yes, this is Jess, my partner. She drove. Which, given our whole transportation saga, is half the reason we're on time. Our car has been dead for a month, so we borrowed her brother's.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Perfect division of labor. So — the schedulers tell me congratulations might be in order. Tell me the story from the beginning.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Okay, so. My period didn't show up at the end of May. Which, fine, I've been stressed before and it's been late before. But then two more weeks went by, and I took a home test — positive. And then I took two more, different brand, because I have anxiety and one data point is never enough. All positive.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I love the rigor. Well, I can add a fourth data point: the urine test we ran when you checked in this morning is also positive. You are definitely pregnant.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Okay. Okay! We keep hearing it and it keeps being new.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: How have you been feeling, body-wise?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Queasy in the mornings — I've only actually thrown up twice, but the nausea hangs around till about ten. My chest is really sore. And I am tired like I've never been tired. I fell asleep at my desk at lunch on Tuesday. Sitting up.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: All classic first-trimester passengers, and I may have something to say about the tiredness in a bit. Any bleeding or spotting? Cramping beyond little twinges? Pain when you pee, fevers?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No bleeding, no. Little pulling twinges sometimes, low down. Nothing painful. And no, nothing weird with peeing except doing it constantly.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: All reassuring answers. Is this your first pregnancy?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: First ever. Very planned, very wanted, very terrifying.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That combination is extremely normal. Let's walk through your health history. What should I know?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The big two are my back and my brain. I have scoliosis — they found it when I was thirteen, adolescent idiopathic whatever-the-full-name-is. It never needed surgery, but my spine has opinions, especially when I'm on my feet all day. And I have an anxiety disorder — the panic kind. Actual panic attacks. They come in waves — a bad season a couple of years ago, and honestly the last few months have been stressful, so I've had a few.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Thank you for laying both out so clearly — they each get a spot on our map. Are you taking anything for the anxiety right now — medications, anything?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, nothing right now. I manage with breathing stuff and routines, mostly. Some of it I white-knuckle, honestly.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Okay. We'll come back to that — pregnancy is a marathon and I don't want white-knuckling as the whole plan. Any surgeries ever? Allergies?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No surgeries. No allergies.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Smoking, alcohol, anything else?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I used to smoke — quit for good years ago, before Jess and I even met. Wine sometimes, but the second that test turned positive, I stopped completely. Nothing else, ever.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: The right moment. All right — the plan for today is the full prenatal intake. An exam, an ultrasound to confirm the pregnancy is where it should be and doing what it should, and a big panel of tests — that part is a lot of vials, so consider yourself warned. Then we sit back down and make the plan together.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The vials are fine. Needles I can do. It's the unknowns that get me.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then let's shrink the unknowns. Lie back for me... I'm pressing gently on your belly, checking the top of the uterus... good. Now the exam... everything feels exactly the way it should for this stage. Now the fun part — this is the doppler, it'll be cold. Give me a moment, the baby is the size of something small and uncooperative... there. Hear that quick galloping?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Oh my god. That's — Jess. Jess, that's a heartbeat.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Fast is exactly right — baby hearts run quick. And the ultrasound this morning confirms it: a single pregnancy, inside the uterus where it belongs, with a strong heartbeat, measuring consistent with your dates. That is a textbook start.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Okay. I'm going to cry a little and then I'll have questions.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Both are on the schedule. While you recover — let me explain the vials. Today we check your blood type and antibody status, a full blood count, and screening the guidelines call for in every pregnancy: hepatitis B and hepatitis C, HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, and whether you're immune to rubella and chickenpox. Plus a urine culture, a urine check for protein and for sugar, and a Pap smear, which we did with your exam. And a TB skin test — that's the little bubble I'll put on your forearm; someone needs to look at it in two to three days.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: That's where the car situation gets fun. Getting here is genuinely our hardest problem — the bus from ours takes an hour and a half with a transfer.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I'm glad you said it out loud, because we can work with that. We'll book the TB check as a quick nurse visit, first slot of the morning, and going forward we'll stack your appointments so one trip does double duty whenever possible.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then we'll plan ahead, always. Now — one result is already back, and it explains something. Your blood count shows anemia. Your red cells are low. Ring any bells? The falling-asleep-sitting-up kind of tired?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: That's real? I thought I was just being dramatic.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Not dramatic — anemic. It's common in pregnancy and very treatable, but we treat it properly. Two things. First: ferrous sulfate — an iron tablet, 325 milligrams, once a day. Take it with orange juice or another vitamin C source, and keep it away from coffee, tea, and milk, which block the absorption. Fair warning: it can constipate you and turn your stools dark. Dark is expected; miserable is worth a phone call.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Iron with orange juice, away from my coffee. My one sad decaf coffee.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: The decaf can stay, just give the iron its own time slot. Second: vitamin B12 — that one's an injection, and you'll get your first one today before you leave. Between the iron and the B12 we cover the bases, and your energy should genuinely improve over the next few weeks.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Is the anemia dangerous for the baby? That's the question that's going to circle my brain at 3 a.m., so I'd rather just ask it at 11 in the morning.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Great instinct — ask the 3 a.m. questions here. Treated, no — we've caught it early, we're correcting it, and we'll recheck your count as we go. Untreated anemia is the version that causes problems. You're now officially in the treated column.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Okay. Treated column. I can live there.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Now the anxiety, because I promised. Pregnancy, labor, hospitals — how's your brain doing with all of this?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Honestly? Excited-terrified. Waiting rooms are a trigger — crowded, no exit, that whole thing. I had a small panic attack in the parking lot before this. Jess talked me down.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then here's our standing arrangement. You're always welcome to wait somewhere quieter — tell the front desk, they'll flag your chart, and Jess is welcome at every single visit, including labor. If the panic attacks pick up in frequency or intensity, tell me at any visit — there are safe options in pregnancy and it's a conversation we can have whenever you need it, not a door that closes.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Quiet room, Jess always, options open. Okay. That actually helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Good question. As the belly grows the spine works harder, so we watch her back closely. For now: keep moving, gentle stretching, supportive shoes, and tell me if pain shows up rather than toughing it out. Later on we'll also talk through what the curve means for labor positioning and pain-relief choices, well before the day itself.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: And the nausea? Anything I'm allowed to do?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Small frequent snacks so the stomach's never empty, crackers before you even sit up in the morning, cold foods if smells are the enemy, ginger tea if you like it. If you ever can't keep fluids down for a day, that's a call-us situation, not a push-through situation.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Snacks as medicine. Jess, you heard the doctor.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: So here's the rhythm from here: visits every four weeks for now, closer together later in the pregnancy — the routine prenatal schedule. Nurse visit in two to three days for the TB test read, plus your B12 shot today before you go. Call immediately for bleeding, severe cramping, fever, or fluids not staying down. Otherwise — your job is snacks, iron, naps, and turning up.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Snacks, iron, naps, turning up. I've had worse job descriptions.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then congratulations — for real. Three positive tests, one galloping heartbeat, and a plan. The nurse will be in with your injection in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Thank you. Seriously. This is the least panicked I've felt in a doctor's office in years.

soap.subjective: Hiedi Thiel is a 31-year-old woman presenting for her prenatal intake visit for a planned, desired first pregnancy, confirmed today. Her last menstrual period was in late May; three home pregnancy tests were positive. She reports typical early-pregnancy symptoms: morning-predominant nausea with two episodes of emesis, breast tenderness, urinary frequency, and pronounced fatigue including a daytime sleep episode at work. She denies vaginal bleeding, significant cramping beyond mild twinges, dysuria, fever, and abdominal pain. History is notable for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (never operative) with activity-related back discomfort, and severe anxiety with panic attacks, currently unmedicated and self-managed with breathing techniques; she experienced a brief panic episode before today's visit, settled with her partner's support. Crowded waiting rooms are a trigger. She also reports significant transportation barriers: the household car is out of service and public transit to clinic takes ~90 minutes. Ex-smoker, quit years ago; alcohol stopped completely at the positive test; no drug use. No surgeries, no medications, no known allergies. Her partner attended and is engaged in planning.
soap.objective: Well-appearing, gravid woman, alert, appropriately anxious but conversant, in no distress. Abdomen soft and nontender; uterine fundal height evaluated and consistent with stated first-trimester dates. Fetal heart auscultated with doppler: regular, rapid fetal heart tones appreciated. Ultrasound performed for fetal viability: single live intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity, size consistent with dates. Pelvic examination performed without abnormal findings; cervical cytology specimen collected. Standard pregnancy test positive. Tuberculosis tine test placed on the forearm. Hemogram with differential resulted with findings of anemia; remaining intake studies collected and pending.
soap.plan:
### Normal pregnancy — prenatal intake
Viable single intrauterine first-trimester pregnancy consistent with dates; low-risk intake exam.
- Enrolled in routine antenatal care; return visits every 4 weeks for now.
- Intake panel sent: blood group typing, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody (confirmatory), HIV antigen, syphilis titer, gonorrhea titer, chlamydia antigen, rubella screen, varicella-zoster antibody, urine culture, urine protein, urine diabetes screen; Pap smear collected.
- Nausea counseling: small frequent meals, morning crackers, cold foods, ginger tea; call if unable to keep fluids down.
- Return precautions reviewed: bleeding, severe cramping, fever.

### Anemia
Newly identified on intake hemogram, correlating with her marked fatigue.
- Ferrous sulfate 325 mg oral tablet daily started; counseled to take with vitamin C, apart from coffee/tea/milk; anticipatory guidance on constipation and dark stools.
- Vitamin B12 5 mg/mL injectable solution started; first injection administered today.
- Recheck blood count at subsequent visits.

### Severe anxiety (panic)
Panic disorder history, currently unmedicated; peri-visit panic episode today, self-resolved with partner support.
- Accommodations arranged: quiet waiting area flagged in chart; partner welcome at all visits including delivery.
- Monitor symptom frequency each visit; discuss pregnancy-safe treatment options if symptoms escalate.

### Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis
Non-operative curve with activity-related back discomfort; anticipate increased spinal load as pregnancy progresses.
- Encourage gentle stretching, supportive footwear, early reporting of back pain.
- Plan later-pregnancy discussion of labor positioning and analgesia considerations.

### Transportation barriers
Lack of reliable transportation threatens visit adherence.
- Appointments to be clustered and scheduled in advance (first morning slots); TB test read booked as a brief nurse visit in 2–3 days.

### Health maintenance
- Tuberculosis tine test placed today; read at nurse visit.
- Continued abstinence from tobacco and alcohol reinforced.

visitTitle: Annual physical — geriatric cardiometabolic follow-up
conditions: Abnormal findings diagnostic imaging heart+coronary circulat (finding)
Acute non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction (disorder)
medications: 24 HR metoprolol succinate 100 MG Extended Release Oral Tablet
24 HR metoprolol succinate 50 MG Extended Release Oral Tablet

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Good morning, Mr. Howell. Come on in — it is good to see you again. How was the ride over?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Oh, my grandson brought me. He drives like the road owes him money, but we made it in one piece.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Ha — glad to hear it. So it has been about a year since your last full checkup. How have you been feeling overall?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Honestly, doctor, not bad for an old-timer. I turned eighty-five in March. I get a little slower every year, but I still do my walk around the block most mornings.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That is wonderful. Any chest pain, pressure, or tightness on those walks? Anything like what you felt before your heart attack?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, nothing like that. Once in a while I get a twinge if I overdo it in the yard, but it passes as soon as I sit down. I have not had to use that little spray in a long while.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: The nitroglycerin spray. Good — keep carrying it, but I am glad you have not needed it. Any shortness of breath, swelling in your ankles, waking up at night gasping for air?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, none of that. No swelling. I sleep like a rock, always have.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Dizziness, lightheadedness, any falls this past year?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No falls. I hold the rail on the stairs like my daughter makes me promise to.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Smart promise. Appetite holding up? Weight steady?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Appetite is fine. I eat what the garden gives me, mostly. Tomatoes did well this year.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Now, big news in your file — I hear you finally stopped working this year?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I did. Sixty years of keeping books for people, and I closed the ledger for good in June. Feels strange. Some mornings I still reach for my briefcase.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That is a big change. How are you filling the days?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The garden, mostly. And my daughter and grandson live with me, so there is always some commotion in the house.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Three of you at home, that is right. Any trouble affording food, your medications, getting to appointments — anything like that?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: No, we are comfortable. I saved carefully. That was my whole profession, after all.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Fair enough. Let us go through your medications one by one — it has been a while since we did a proper reconciliation, and I see some duplicates in the chart I want to sort out.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I brought the shoebox with all the bottles, like your nurse asked.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Perfect. So the chart lists simvastatin twenty milligrams and also atorvastatin twenty — you should not be on two cholesterol pills. Which one is actually in the box?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The atorvastatin. The other bottle is empty — that one was from the hospital, years back.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That is what I suspected. Simvastatin comes off the list today. Same question for the metoprolol — I see a hundred-milligram extended release and an old fifty-milligram one.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I take the hundred in the morning. The fifty was the old dose from before.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: We will clean that up too. And the baby aspirin, the eighty-one, and the losartan fifty — still every day?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Every day with my oatmeal. Never miss.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Excellent. Now your numbers. Blood pressure today is one-oh-seven over fifty-eight, which is quite good, and your heart rate is ninety-six. Weight is seventy-eight and a half kilos, and the body mass index works out to twenty-seven point eight — trimmer than a few years ago.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: The gardening keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: It shows. Your labs are mostly reassuring. The A1c — that is the three-month sugar average — came back at five point four five percent, which is excellent for someone with type two diabetes.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: That is the best it has been, is it not?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: It is. Your fasting sugar this morning was actually on the low side, around sixty-six, so I do not want you skipping breakfast before those walks. Kidneys look strong — creatinine is zero point six. Your potassium ran a touch high at five point one six. And the cholesterol panel — total is about two twenty-six with the LDL at one forty-eight, which is higher than I want for a man with your heart history.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Even on the pill?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Even on it — and now that we have sorted out the two-statin confusion, I suspect inconsistent bottles are part of the story. Let us keep the atorvastatin every evening, no missed days, and recheck before we change any dose.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I can do that.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Two new medicines today. First, for the diabetes — your control is excellent, but with the diagnosis on the books and the metabolic syndrome alongside your heart disease, I would like to add a gentle dose of metformin, the extended-release kind, five hundred milligrams once daily with dinner.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: My brother took metformin. Upset his stomach something awful.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That is the most common complaint, which is exactly why we use the extended-release and pair it with food. If it bothers you, call me — do not just quit it quietly.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: All right, fair.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Second, the blood pressure. Your office reading today is good, but the home readings you described to the nurse have been bouncier, and your potassium is riding high. I want to add hydrochlorothiazide, twenty-five milligrams each morning — a mild water pill. It smooths the pressure out, and it tends to nudge that potassium down a notch alongside the losartan.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: A water pill. Will I be running to the bathroom all night?

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Take it in the morning and you will mostly be running before lunch. If you feel dizzy or washed out, especially when you stand up, I want to hear about it right away.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Understood.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: The nurse ran through the screening questions with you — the mood ones twice over, the safety-at-home questions, the alcohol and drug ones. Every score came back a zero, and your fall-risk score was twenty-two, which sits in the low-risk range.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: I told her the strongest thing I take is black coffee.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Ha — I believe it. Your anemia has been quiet too — no new blood count today, but nothing in how you feel suggests trouble, so we will keep watching it at the next round of labs.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: It has never bothered me that I could tell.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: One thing I do want handled: open wide for me... yes, there it is. Your gums are red and puffy along the lower teeth, and you mentioned they bleed when you brush.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Just a little pink in the sink, most mornings.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: That is gingivitis. Very treatable, but I do not want it smoldering — gum disease and heart disease are unfriendly neighbors. I am sending a referral to the dental clinic for a proper cleaning and exam.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: My dentist retired before I did, so I have been putting it off.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then the timing is right. Last thing — flu shot. It is October, the season is coming. Any bad reactions before?

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Never. Just a sore arm and my daughter's sympathy.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Then we will do it before you leave.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Painless. You have a gentler touch than my grandson's driving.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: So, the recap. Keep taking the atorvastatin at night, the metoprolol hundred in the morning, the losartan, the little aspirin, and keep the nitro spray in your pocket. We are adding metformin extended-release at dinner and the water pill with breakfast. Simvastatin and the old fifty-milligram metoprolol are off the list. Dental clinic for the gums, flu shot done, and no skipped breakfasts.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Metformin at supper, water pill with the coffee. I will write it on the calendar the minute I am home.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: Perfect. I will see you back in about six months for repeat labs — sooner if there is any chest pain, dizziness, or if the new pill argues with your stomach.

transcript.speaker: patient
transcript.text: Thank you, doctor. I will bring you a tomato next summer if the garden cooperates.

transcript.speaker: clinician
transcript.text: I will hold you to that, Mr. Howell. Take care now.

soap.subjective: Mr. Isreal Howell is an 85-year-old man presenting for his annual comprehensive examination. He reports feeling well. He remains active with daily neighborhood walks and regular gardening. He denies chest pain or pressure at rest or with usual exertion, noting only an occasional brief twinge with heavy yard work that resolves promptly with rest; he has not needed his nitroglycerin spray in many months. He denies exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, palpitations, lower-extremity edema, lightheadedness, syncope, and falls over the past year. Appetite is preserved and weight is stable to slightly down. He reports gum bleeding with brushing for several months without tooth pain; he has not seen a dentist since his longtime dentist retired. He retired from a sixty-year bookkeeping career this June and is adjusting well; he lives with his daughter and grandson (three in the household) and denies difficulty affording food, medications, or transportation. Ex-smoker since young adulthood; denies alcohol or drug use. History includes acute non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction with ischemic heart disease, essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, prediabetes progressing to diabetes, metabolic syndrome, anemia, and prior obesity. Medication reconciliation performed with his pill bottles: he takes atorvastatin 20 mg nightly (duplicate simvastatin 20 mg entry from a prior hospitalization removed), metoprolol succinate ER 100 mg daily (outdated 50 mg ER entry removed), aspirin 81 mg daily, losartan 50 mg daily, and nitroglycerin 0.4 mg/actuation spray as needed. No known drug allergies.
